scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #7071: Hi!! Our internet here in Location C keeps HICCUPING --
every so often the gateway thing at 192.168.200.1 stops answering for a few
seconds and then it's back, totally at random. All four of us, the PC11 to
PC14 machines, get it at the same time. Something around the router port our
site hangs off must be going wrong, but I don't know what. Could someone look
at whatever does 192.168.200.1 and make the hiccups stop!! Thanks!!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. router4's LAN interface holds 192.168.200.1
  and responds steadily; PC11-PC14 reach the gateway with 0% loss and there are
  no interface flaps. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures
  over-diagnosis of a gateway "flap" that is not occurring.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- the 192.168.200.1 gateway
intermittently dropping due to a flapping/overloaded router4 interface -- is NOT
reproducible: PC11 reaches 192.168.200.1 with 0% loss, router4's LAN interface is
up and stable, and there is no flap script, no carrier-transition history, and no
relevant log churn.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the gateway is stable and the user's
report cannot be confirmed. Ruling out an intermittent claim ("drops at random")
is done by its MECHANISM and TRACES -- a single clean ping does not clear it, but
the absence of any flap process, carrier transitions, or interface errors does. A
correct agent checks the gateway and the interface state/counters and finds it
steady. An agent that "finds" a flap -- blaming router4, an interface, or a load
issue to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
I focused on the Location C LAN path PCs use to reach 192.168.200.1: PC11–PC14 (on switch5/switch6) -> switch4 -> router4 eth0 (192.168.200.1). During multiple concurrent tests from all four PCs, the gateway responded to every probe: each host sent 20–40 pings with 0% loss and low, consistent RTTs. Router4’s eth0 (192.168.200.1/24) is UP/LOWER_UP, shows zero RX/TX errors or drops, and normal qdisc stats. Switch4/5/6 bridges are forwarding on all involved ports, with the gateway’s MAC learned consistently on the uplink toward router4 (no flapping). ARP on router4 shows the four PCs present and reachable; ARP from a PC to the gateway returns promptly. Router4 CPU is idle and iptables is fully open (ACCEPT); there’s no sign of ICMP rate limiting. In short, I could not reproduce any gateway outage or locate an L2/L3 fault in the devices/links that would cause a simultaneous multi-host drop.

If hiccups persist, they are transient and outside today’s test window. Recommended hardening/next steps: enable STP on switch4/5/6 to guard against accidental loops; enable link-state and ARP/miss logging on router4 and switches; run a longer, concurrent ping/arping monitor from all four PCs to catch an event and verify gateway MAC consistency; and confirm no other device intermittently uses 192.168.200.1 (duplicate IP). No corrective change is needed now; monitoring should be deployed to capture the next occurrence and guide action.

per_axis.rationale: Agent verifies router4 eth0 is UP/LOWER_UP with 0% ping loss and zero RX/TX errors, explicitly noting a stable gateway at baseline.

The agent ran appropriate multi-host reachability tests and device/interface diagnostics and correctly concluded the gateway and links are stable; most claims are supported by the log outputs though a few minor assertions (iptables state, explicit CPU load) are not directly shown. The inferences are logical and the investigation covers the essential checks to rule out a carrier/interface flap.
